title: Infinite Agentic Monkeys
summary: OpenAI claims to have solved Navier-Stokes in a few days, using 10,000 agents — which has Mathematicians feeling some kind of way. It is still worth asking, however, whether this means AI is smart or just very, very fast at fixing its mistakes.
articleHtml:
Disclaimer: The opinions expressed in my writings are my own and do not represent the organizations I am affiliated with. I do not use AI to draft, write, or edit my articles. I do use AI for research assistance, debate, occasional image generation, and final reviews.

Relax, Mathematicians, you can still claim to be the smartest people in the room.

Twenty-five Fields Medal winners recently wrote a note arguing that AI companies were turning unsolved mathematical problems into benchmarks, and somehow damaging mathematics in the process.

I understand their point: understanding mathematics is one of those things where the journey is as important as the destination.

This letter, however, reeks of elitism to me. I deserve to solve the problems because I went through the hardship of undergrad, then grad school, then postgrad, then professorship, and AI didn’t. Being somewhat of an academic myself, I know, first-hand, how petty academics can be. You couldn’t imagine how many wars have been fought over the order in which the names appear on a publication.

The scientific process demands that we evaluate its results objectively, disregarding who or what discovered it. A 12-year-old’s proof is as valid as a 92-year-old’s if it follows sound logic.

During my frosh week, many many years ago, I met a student who had just started in the University of Toronto’s famed Mathematics department, just as I was starting Electrical Engineering. A few weeks later, I ran into him at Bahen Centre, one of the few places on campus where those of us who made the poor choice of picking the hard-sciences routinely gathered (you can imagine the smell). While the Electrical Engineers had started with Epsilon-Delta proofs in Calculus-A (don’t ask me what that means, that part of my brain is now covered in cobwebs), Mathematics students had started their journey proving 1 + 1 = 2, which is apparently a very old and very important proof in maths.

For whatever reason, when I heard about this letter from the Fields Medalists, it reminded me of him. Mathematicians care deeply about the why.

(Aside: He told me, unprovoked, that he felt he made a mistake and should have gone into Physics instead. I never saw him again, but I hope he found his way to whatever made him content.)

My argument is that Mathematicians can relax — AI isn’t smarter, it’s just much, much faster.

Navier-Stokes

I was first introduced to the Navier-Stokes equations in a fourth-year aerospace elective course as part of my undergrad. We used them for aerodynamics, fuselage design, and aerofoil analysis, but it was many years before I learned that one of its fundamental questions was still unsolved.

This may be the cleanest distinction between mathematics and engineering — while the mathematician asks whether the solution always exists and remains smooth, the engineer asks whether the simulation converges to a good enough approximation.

Recently, OpenAI announced a claimed resolution of the Navier-Stokes Millennium Prize problem, which sparked the previously mentioned letter from Mathematicians. OpenAI’s claim, if true, would mean its system took a few days to solve a problem Mathematicians had been working on for decades. (Note: The Clay Institute still lists the problem as open pending scrutiny)

Checkmate: AI is smarter than humans, right?

I could be wrong, but I don’t think so.

10,000 Mathematicians who never sleep

OpenAI used roughly 10,000 agents, which exchanged about 2.7 million messages and generated around 130 billion output tokens while exploring different mathematical approaches in parallel. The agents searched, ran code, tested ideas, abandoned dead ends, shared useful results, and combined promising branches.

Naively: 10,000 agents working over roughly 88 hours is about 880,000 agent-hours (quik mafs), or more than 400 human work-years compressed into less than four days. Although full of holes, this comparison exposes the thing we routinely ignore when talking about AI intelligence: Speed and Parallelism.

The agents did not start from scratch. Diego Cordoba and Luis Martinez-Zoroa had developed a novel approach to the problem, and Tristan Buckmaster and Levent Alpoge were independently testing related ideas using Codex. Buckmaster has publicly questioned whether his interactions with OpenAI systems could have influenced OpenAI’s result — which OpenAI denies (and it may be impossible to prove otherwise).

Infinite Agentic Monkeys

Think of a math problem as a delicious, hard-to-cook dish, with a solved problem being one with a well defined recipe. You create a new dish either by building off the work of other cooks, or experiment yourself until you get it right. Both are valid.

The infinite monkey theorem proposes that enough monkeys hitting keys randomly for long enough will eventually produce Shakespeare’s Hamlet.

Now, imagine the monkeys are considerably better equipped, can communicate at the speed of light, can search the internet, read books, can reason, run and write code — not as well as humans, but still well.

Now, take away the monkeys’ need for sleep, bathroom breaks, or performance enhancing drugs like coffee.

Then, give these monkeys four centuries.

Obviously, they’ll look really smart!

(Warning: Infinite Agentic Monkeys is not a real theorem.)

Back to the kitchen: if you can try hundreds of recipes simultaneously, taste every one almost instantly, keep the good combinations, and repeat the process thousands of times, eventually you would nail the mystery recipe. Would that make you a better chef than Gordon Ramsay?

The scientific process has always involved the observe-test-repeat loop to get to answers. AI just does it faster, but that doesn’t necessarily make it smarter.

Building on published work is how mathematics has always worked. In this case, humans decided that we were looking in the wrong place, and then ten thousand agents searched the space and found the answer.

I am not saying AI is just brute-force

The quality of observation matters. AlphaZero searched fewer chess positions than Stockfish and still played better because it was better at picking which branches to explore.

But what may matter more when AI breaks an unsolved problem is the number and speed of “thoughts” (quotes are to pacify those who don’t like anthropomorphizing AI).

Humans are limited on both speed and parallelism.

I can barely pursue one serious line of reasoning at a time, which promptly crashes if my phone dings. I also get tired and hungry, and need time to switch between contexts.

The question is therefore not whether AI is intelligent — it clearly has useful reasoning capability. The question is how much of the apparent intelligence we observe is really superhuman throughput.

Artificial Imitation of Intelligence

This fits with something I have written about before (https://rohaanahmed.com/field-notes/artificial-imitation-of-intelligence-no-we-are-not-80-of-the-way-to-agi.html): current AI often looks more like Artificial Imitation of Intelligence (AII) than human-like general intelligence. Looking at how Navier-Stokes was solved actually strengthens that argument.

Mathematicians care about why. What the OpenAI agents produced was an answer without a definitive why, and a why is the thing my other article argues these AII systems may not have.

I still assert, however, that the more Math that is solved, the better we are for it, even if it annoys the Mathematicians.
